Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

What is the average vacation package price right now?

The average tracked vacation package price is $301 and the median is $199. The gap between the two matters: a handful of premium all-inclusive and cruise packages pull the average upward, while most of what you can actually book clusters near the median. If you want a realistic budget number, use the median — half of all live deals sit below $199.

The Vacation Package Price Index is built from every deal our crawlers currently track: 617 active listings, 35 brands, and 80 destinations, backed by 74,440 historical price observations. We recompute the index whenever a source re-prices, so the number you see is never more than a few hours stale. Browse the live inventory any time on the all-deals page.

How prices moved this month

Prices stayed broadly flat month over month, with the median holding near $199 and the cheapest live deal landing at $48.86 (a PayVibe Williamsburg package). The most reliable way to read movement is not the average — it is the floor. The $49 price floor has held remarkably steady across markets, and 168 of our 617 deals are currently priced under $100.

Cheapest market today

How to read the index like an analyst

Three numbers do most of the work. The median ($199) is your budget anchor — plan around it, not the average. The average ($301) tells you how much premium inventory (all-inclusive, cruise, air-inclusive) is skewing the market; a rising average with a flat median means more luxury listings, not a worse deal for you. The price per night ($94) is the only fair way to compare a one-night stay against a five-night package. Watch all three together and a single advertised quote stops being mysterious — you can immediately place it as cheap, average, or premium.

The spread matters as much as the midpoint. Any one advertised price can be a loss leader or an outlier. Last updated July 2026 · based on 74,440 tracked price observations across 617 active vacation deals.

What is the average price of a timeshare presentation package?

The average price of a timeshare presentation package is $301, and the median is $199. "Presentation deals" are discounted vacation packages you get in exchange for attending a resort's sales presentation — usually 90 to 120 minutes. Our data shows the average disclosed presentation length is 116 minutes, and 47% of tracked deals openly state that a presentation is required (the rest bundle it less visibly).

Because a small number of premium all-inclusive and cruise packages sit in the four figures, the median is the more useful number for budgeting. Half of the 617 deals we track are priced below $199, and 168 are under $100. See the full live list on the deals page, or the market-wide Price Index.

Average price by brand

Brand is the single biggest driver of price. Budget broker brands like VacationVIP and PayVibe average under $120, while premium sellers like Departure Depot and Marriott run several times higher because they bundle flights or all-inclusive resorts.

Average price by destination

Destination matters almost as much as brand. Gatlinburg averages just $141, while Cancun averages $533 because those packages are all-inclusive. The floor, though, is nearly identical everywhere: $49–$51 in Orlando, Las Vegas, Branson, Gatlinburg, Myrtle Beach, and Williamsburg alike. For per-market detail, see the price-history pages for Orlando, Las Vegas, and Gatlinburg, or shop a specific brand like Westgate. To compare true value across lengths, use the price-per-night rankings.

Why the average and median differ so much

The $102 gap between the $301 average and the $199 median is not noise — it is the signature of a two-tier market. On one side sit hundreds of budget preview packages anchored to a $49 floor; on the other, a smaller set of premium bundles from brands like Departure Depot ($969 average) and Marriott ($590) that fold in airfare or all-inclusive resorts. A simple average blends those two populations into a number that describes neither well. The median ignores the luxury tail and lands where most bookable deals actually are, which is why it is the figure to plan around.

This also explains why "average price" headlines can be misleading elsewhere on the web. A site that quotes only the mean makes vacation packages look pricier than they are for a typical traveler. By publishing the median, the floor, and per-brand detail side by side, we let you see that a sub-$200 package is not a rare markdown — it is the middle of the market. Compare any quote against the Price Index to see instantly where it falls.

What you actually pay for

The package price buys discounted lodging; the "cost" is your time in the presentation. Nearly half of deals disclose that requirement up front, and typical eligibility rules apply — usually age 25+, a household income around $50K+, a valid credit card, and (for couples' rates) both partners attending. Knowing the average price protects you from overpaying: if a package is quoted far above $301 without all-inclusive or airfare, ask what is actually bundled. Which vacation deals dropped the most?

The largest verified markdown this month is the Charleston Food & Wine getaway, down $400 (from $1,699 to $1,299). How we verify drops (and reject data artifacts)

Not every price change is a real drop. Our crawlers occasionally misread a page — a currency glitch, a placeholder value, or a stale cache can make a price look like it collapsed when it did not. Before a drop appears on this leaderboard, it has to clear several checks:

  • Both prices must be independently observed in our snapshot history, not inferred from a single reading.
  • Implausible collapses are rejected. A package that appears to fall from four figures to under $200 in one step is flagged as a likely scraper artifact and withheld until a human confirms it. We are actively correcting a batch of such false entries and deliberately do not cite them here.

Key fact: If a drop looks too good to be true — like a 90% overnight collapse — it usually is a data artifact, not a bargain. We hold those back rather than mislead you. Only clean, persistent, independently observed drops make this page.

The biggest verified drops share a pattern: they are premium, higher-priced packages, not floor deals. A $49 preview stay has almost no room to fall, but a $1,699 Charleston getaway or a $1,299 cruise has real margin to discount when a departure date approaches or inventory needs to move. That is why the leaderboard skews toward four-figure packages — the dollar swings are simply larger up there. A $400 drop on a $1,699 deal is a 24% cut; the same $400 could never come off a $49 room.

This is also why percentage and dollar terms tell different stories. The AC/DC Atlanta package dropped the smallest dollar amount ($300) but the largest percentage (33%), making it arguably the best relative value of the three. When you scan a price-drop list, read both columns: dollars tell you how much you save, percentage tells you how deep the discount is relative to the original price.

One more thing the leaderboard is not: a promise that a price will keep falling. A verified drop tells you a brand chose to discount once, not that it will do so again. Premium packages like these can just as easily tick back up when a departure date fills, so treat a confirmed markdown as a reason to act, not a signal to wait for an even lower number that may never arrive.

How to put a real dollar value on a presentation gift

The honest way to value any incentive is to convert everything to dollars and subtract what you would have paid anyway. Start with the room: take the package price and compare it to the $301 market average or, better, the per-night average of $94. The difference is your real "room gift." Then add cash-equivalent extras at full value, tickets only if you had already planned to buy them, and points at a conservative discount. What you are left with is the offer's true worth — usually far more grounded than the "retail value" printed in the ad.

Be skeptical of inflated retail-value claims. A package that touts "$915 value" but sits at a $199 price is telling you about a sticker figure, not the market. Our tracked averages are the antidote: if the stated value is wildly above what comparable stays actually cost, discount it. The incentive is still real — it is just smaller than advertised, and knowing the gap keeps you from booking a mediocre deal because the "value" number looked big.

Finally, weigh the gift against your own time. If a deal hands you a $100 gift card and a stay $150 below market in exchange for a 116-minute presentation, you are effectively being paid a few hundred dollars for two hours — a genuinely good trade for many travelers. If the incentives are mostly soft points and hard-to-use tickets, the math is thinner. The tracker exists so you can run that calculation on real numbers instead of the marketing copy.

Cash vs points vs tickets: which is best?

Cash-equivalent gift cards are the easiest to value — a dollar is a dollar. Tickets are worth their face value only if you would have bought them anyway. Points are the softest currency: their real value depends on the redemption program, so treat a points incentive conservatively. The most reliable value is the discount on the room itself, which you can verify against the price-per-night rankings.

Key fact: The gift is only free if the presentation is. Budget 90–120 minutes (116 on average when disclosed) and confirm eligibility — usually age 25+, household income around $50K+, both partners of a couple attending, and a valid credit card.

Which brands reprice most often?

Stable vs jumpy brands

Brands fall into two camps. "Jumpy" brands carry high inventory and reprice frequently around a low floor. "Stable" brands post a fixed promotional rate and hold it — you can see this in their data, where the cheapest and average prices are nearly identical.

Fixed-rate sellers take the opposite approach: they publish one promotional price, often $199, and hold it because their goal is a clean, predictable offer rather than a race to the floor. Inventory count is the tell. Brands with dozens or hundreds of listings almost always show a wide floor-to-average spread, because a large catalog naturally spans budget and premium tiers and gets repriced often. Brands with a handful of listings tend to show a narrow spread — fewer deals, less repricing, a steadier posted rate. That relationship is why our snapshot cadence matters: only by observing the same deals repeatedly across 74,440 total readings can we separate a brand that is genuinely stable from one we simply have not watched long enough.

There is a competitive dimension too. Volatility clusters in the most contested markets, where several brokers sell overlapping inventory and nudge prices to win the top slot in a sorted list. In markets or brands with little competition, prices sit still because there is no rival forcing a response. So when you see a brand repricing constantly, read it as a sign of a healthy, competitive corner of the market — the kind of place where patience and a daily check are most likely to be rewarded with a floor price.

What volatility means for buyers

A wide gap between a brand's cheapest and average price — Westgate's $49 floor under a $201 average — is the fingerprint of a jumpy brand. It signals that patience pays: waiting for the floor can save well over $100. A narrow spread, like Capital Vacations at $199 cheapest and $199 average, means there is nothing to wait for; the posted price is the price.

Why day-of-week pricing doesn't apply here

Day-of-week pricing exists in industries that use revenue management — airlines and standard hotels constantly adjust rates based on real-time demand for a specific date. A timeshare-preview package is a different animal. Its price is a fixed marketing cost: the brand decides that a $49 or $199 offer is what it takes to seat someone in a presentation, and that figure is set well in advance of any particular check-in date. There is no algorithm nudging it up for a Saturday, because the room is not the product being sold — the presentation slot is.

This is why our snapshots show a flat floor across the week. If demand-based pricing were at work, the cheapest observed price would dip on low-demand midweek dates and spike on weekends. Instead it holds near $49–$51 regardless. The only genuine downward moves we record are brand-initiated markdowns — the kind that land on our price-drop leaderboard — and those happen on their own schedule, not on a predictable weekday cycle you can game.

That said, the weekday advantage is real in one respect: getting the trip you want. Because many preview packages require or prefer midweek check-ins and exclude peak weekends, travelers who can start their stay on a Tuesday or Wednesday face fewer blackout dates and a wider choice of resorts. You are not paying less per night, but you are far more likely to actually secure the floor-priced deal on the dates you want. For flexible travelers, that availability edge is worth more than any imagined day-of-week discount.

Booking-day myths tested

A related myth says booking on a specific weekday (often "Tuesday") unlocks a lower price. For preview packages that does not apply — the promotional rate is set in advance and does not fluctuate by the day you click "book." That myth comes from airfare and revenue-managed hotel pricing, which these fixed-rate packages are not. If you see a lower price on any given day, it is a genuine price change from the brand (track those on the price-drop leaderboard), not a day-of-week trick.

Key fact: The lever that actually saves money is not the day — it is the destination and brand. Gatlinburg ($141 average) versus Cancun ($533) moves your cost far more than any weekday-versus-weekend choice ever will.
